cells.tense: Something is ending and you're the one letting it end.
cells.ask: Finish the one thing you can name as done, and say what it was for before you clear the space it leaves.
cells.core:
You can tell what's finished. Not by reasoning it out — the things that have already given what they had are the ones you're releasing, at the pace they ask for. That's the whole skill here. What deserves your attention and what stopped deserving it are both plain to you.

The endings you make are clean because you're not ending anything you're still inside. When you let one go it's because it's over, not because it got hard. So the space it leaves is usable. What comes next doesn't have to fight the old thing for room, and you don't have to call the old thing a mistake to move on from it.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished, and you let it finish.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes can arrive
cells.place: Where what deserves your attention is known before it can be argued

cells.tense: You're already clearing rooms you haven't lived in yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been about to end and give it a fixed date to prove itself by — then do nothing until that date arrives.
cells.core:
You've been ending things early. Not wrong things, necessarily — things that hadn't finished, ended ahead of time because ending them felt like moving. The clearing has become the thing you do. Every situation gets scanned for what needs to go, and you find it, because anything can be made to look like dead weight if you're looking.

The part that's hard to say: some of this is fear wearing the clothes of freedom. Leaving first means not getting left. You're standing in front of a future you can't write, bracing for it, and calling the bracing a fresh start. What gets cleared that way doesn't stay clear. You fill it back up and start scanning again.
cells.sheetLine: Ending things early has become its own kind of staying still.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes can arrive
cells.place: Where what deserves your attention is known before it can be argued

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that closed behind you well before now.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you're keeping out of loyalty, and take one small step that assumes it's over — a box packed, a call not made back.
cells.core:
Something ended and you didn't. You kept the shape of it — kept showing up where it used to be, kept the obligations that only made sense while it was alive. You can still see what it was, and you've been treating that picture as the thing itself.

Meanwhile the rest of your life still gets your attention. It's just not this. What's worth your time is plain to you everywhere except here, where the answer is obvious and you're not looking at it. No force will move this. What moves it is the first bit of motion from something you actually feel — and even a small one starts the current.
cells.sheetLine: You kept the commitment after the thing it belonged to was gone.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes can arrive

cells.tense: The room is changing and you're describing it as weather.
cells.ask: Write down the three things you gave the most time to last month, and mark the one you keep explaining rather than choosing.
cells.core:
There's a part of your life you keep narrating as circumstance. It shows in how you talk about it — the sigh, the explaining, the way you file it under conditions instead of under your own decisions. What you're describing as something happening to you is something you're choosing to keep.

Things are ending in your life either way, whether or not you say so, and the ones you're not naming are ending messier — slower, with more debris, because nobody is minding the clearing. You're not missing the ability to see it. You're just not being the one who says it first.
cells.sheetLine: Things are ending that you haven't admitted are ending.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that an ending is underway in their life at all — especially hard in Too Little, where my draft shows someone mid-refusal, and the reader could rightly say nothing is currently dying and the loyalty is simply loyalty. The ask still works if I have that wrong, because naming what you're steering by and what no longer steers your days is useful whether or not a death is in progress. The sentence that serves me more than them is a clean balanced line about endings arriving with a shape; the person has no obligation to be there yet, so I've kept the diagnosis of the moment as what they can see rather than a report on their history.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that an ending is actually underway in their life — in Too Little and Unacknowledged especially, the reader could rightly say nothing is dying and the loyalty is simply loyalty. The ask survives being wrong either way: sorting what you actually attend to, and naming what you keep re-explaining instead of choosing, is useful whether or not a death is in progress. The sentence that serves me more than them is any clean balanced line about endings arriving with a shape; the person owes me no such moment, so I keep the read on what they can look at now, never on what happened to them.
